solution.concept_anchor: Article 243ZD constitutional placement and amendment
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students often confuse Part IX-A (Municipalities) with Part IX-B and may believe DPCs are under the Municipalities chapter since DPCs integrate urban plans.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Part IX-A governs Municipalities (Articles 243P–243ZG), not DPCs specifically under 243ZD — DPC falls within this Part.
Eliminate (c): Part IX governs Panchayats (Articles 243–243O); DPC is NOT in Part IX.
Eliminate (d): The 73rd Amendment deals exclusively with Panchayats; the source for DPC is the 74th Amendment.
Confirm (b): Article 243ZD is in Part IX-A, inserted by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently confuse Part IX (Panchayats) and Part IX-A (Municipalities + DPC + MPC) because DPCs deal with both rural and urban planning. The trap here is that Article 243ZD, while covering a body that integrates Panchayat plans, is itself located in Part IX-A, not Part IX. A student who memorises only that 'Panchayat = Part IX' may wrongly select option (c). Additionally, the 73rd vs 74th Amendment distinction is a perennial UPSC trap — 74th, not 73rd, inserted DPC provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 inserted Part IX-A into the Constitution, covering Articles 243P through 243ZG. This Part deals with Municipalities, but also includes the District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD) and Metropolitan Planning Committee (Article 243ZE).

• Option (a): Incorrect framing — though 243ZD is in Part IX-A, the option incorrectly attributes it to the 73rd Amendment.
• Option (b): Correct. Article 243ZD is in Part IX-A, introduced by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Part IX governs Panchayats (Articles 243–243O) and does not contain DPC provisions.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The 73rd Amendment inserted Part IX (Panchayats); the 74th inserted Part IX-A including DPC.

Value Addition:
• The 73rd and 74th Amendments were passed simultaneously in December 1992 and came into force in April 1993.
• Article 243ZD uses the word 'shall' — making DPC constitution mandatory, not discretionary.
• Both the 73rd and 74th Amendments are landmark constitutional changes adding Part IX and Part IX-A respectively.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC elected member fraction and rural-urban proportion

statement_analysis.statement: At least four-fifths of the members of a District Planning Committee must be elected from amongst the members of Panchayats and Municipalities in the district.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZD(2) explicitly prescribes that not less than four-fifths (4/5) of total members shall be elected from Panchayat and Municipal members in the district.

statement_analysis.statement: The proportion of seats for members elected from Panchayats and Municipalities shall be determined solely by the state legislature without any constitutional guidance.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution itself provides guidance: the proportion shall be in ratio to the rural and urban populations in the district — state legislature must follow this constitutional criterion.

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution permits up to one-fifth of DPC members to be nominated, making it not a fully elected body.
statement_analysis.reason: Since at least 4/5 must be elected, the remaining up to 1/5 can be nominated — the Constitution does not require 100% elected composition.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students aware that DPCs are representative bodies may assume the rural-urban proportion is entirely left to state discretion, when in fact the Constitution provides the criterion of population ratio.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Article 243ZD(2) uses 'not less than four-fifths' — exact constitutional fraction, Statement 1 is correct.
Reject Statement 2: The Constitution does provide guidance — the Panchayat-to-Municipality seat ratio must reflect the rural-urban population ratio, not purely state discretion.
Confirm Statement 3: 4/5 elected implies up to 1/5 may be nominated — DPC is constitutionally not a fully elected body.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap. Students who know that state legislatures are given flexibility in operationalising DPCs may overgeneralise this and assume the rural-urban seat proportion is also fully left to states. In reality, the Constitution explicitly mandates that this proportion must reflect the actual rural-urban population ratio in the district — a specific constitutional criterion that limits state discretion on this particular point.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243ZD(2) lays down specific rules for DPC composition. The constitutional minimum for elected members is four-fifths of the total strength — these must be elected from amongst Panchayat and Municipal members. The remaining up to one-fifth can be nominated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 4/5 threshold is directly stated in Article 243ZD(2). This is a high-yield constitutional fraction.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Constitution is not silent on the internal proportion. It mandates that Panchayat seats vs Municipality seats must reflect the rural-to-urban population ratio in the district — this is a constitutional, not purely legislative, requirement.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The permissibility of nominated members is implied by the 4/5 floor — up to 1/5 may be nominated. DPCs are therefore mixed bodies, not purely elected.

Value Addition:
• The 4/5 elected fraction for DPC is more stringent than MPC (which requires only 2/3 elected) — a common comparison trap.
• Nominated members in DPC are typically state government nominees or technical experts depending on state law.
• This composition reflects the constitutional intent to make DPC a representative body while retaining executive input.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC consolidation function vs independent planning

statement_analysis.statement: The District Planning Committee independently prepares a comprehensive development plan for the district from scratch, without relying on plans submitted by Panchayats and Municipalities.
statement_analysis.reason: DPC's constitutional function is to consolidate plans prepared by Panchayats and Municipalities — it does not independently prepare plans from scratch.

statement_analysis.statement: The draft development plan prepared by the DPC covers only the rural areas of the district, leaving urban planning to the Metropolitan Planning Committee.
statement_analysis.reason: The DPC's draft plan must cover the entire district including both rural and urban areas; it integrates plans of both Panchayats and Municipalities.

statement_analysis.statement: Once the DPC finalises its draft development plan, it has constitutional authority to approve and implement it without requiring state government ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 243ZD(3), the Chairperson must forward the draft plan to the state government; DPC has no final approval or implementation authority.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know DPC prepares plans may assume Statement 1 alone is incorrect while believing Statement 2 about urban coverage has some truth given that MPCs separately handle metro areas.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: DPC consolidates local body plans — it does not originate plans independently.
Statement 2 is incorrect: DPC covers BOTH rural and urban areas; urban-only bodies like MPC exist only for metropolitan areas, not as a substitute for DPC urban coverage.
Statement 3 is incorrect: The Chairperson forwards the plan to the state government; no constitutional authority exists for DPC to self-approve or implement.
All three statements are incorrect — answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the student's knowledge of MPCs. Knowing that Metropolitan Planning Committees exist for urban areas, a student may incorrectly conclude that DPC handles only rural planning. In reality, DPC's integrative mandate specifically covers both rural (Panchayat) and urban (Municipal) areas of the district. MPCs exist for metropolitan cities but do not cover all urban areas in a district, and DPC's constitutional mandate is explicitly district-wide.
solution.final_explanation:
The DPC's constitutional function is consolidation and integration, not independent planning. This distinction is fundamental to understanding Article 243ZD.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: DPC consolidates plans already prepared by Panchayats and Municipalities. It is a coordinating-integrating body, not an originating planning body.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The DPC's draft plan must encompass the entire district — both rural areas governed by Panchayats and urban areas governed by Municipalities. DPC is the only body constitutionally mandated to integrate both.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 243ZD(3) requires the Chairperson to forward the draft plan to the state government. The Constitution is silent on what the state must do thereafter — but DPC itself has no approval or implementation authority.

Value Addition:
• DPC is the only constitutional body at the district level integrating rural-urban plans.
• The state government's silence obligation after receiving the DPC plan is a noted implementation weakness.
• The 2nd ARC recommended giving DPCs formal powers to approve district plans to cure this structural gap.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC vs MPC structural differences elected threshold

statement_analysis.statement: DPC is governed by Article 243ZD while MPC is governed by Article 243ZE — both inserted by the 74th Constitutional Amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZD (DPC) and Article 243ZE (MPC) are both in Part IX-A introduced by the 74th Amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum proportion of elected members required in a DPC (4/5) is higher than that required in an MPC (2/3).
statement_analysis.reason: DPC requires at least 4/5 elected members; MPC requires at least 2/3 elected members — DPC has a higher elected-member threshold.

statement_analysis.statement: MPC is constituted for areas with a population of 10 lakh or more, while DPC is constituted at the district level regardless of population threshold.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZE mandates MPCs for metropolitan areas (population ≥ 10 lakh); DPC under Article 243ZD applies at district level without a population floor.

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution specifies that the Chairperson of both DPC and MPC shall be an elected representative from amongst the members of the respective committee.
statement_analysis.reason: For DPC, the Constitution does NOT specify who shall be Chairperson — it is left to state legislature. Only for MPC is the Chairperson typically envisaged as an elected representative.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) suggesting only two are correct is deceptive because Statement 4 about Chairperson appointment sounds authoritative enough that students might accept it, reducing the correct count to two.
elimination_logic: Confirm Pair 1: Article 243ZD (DPC) and 243ZE (MPC), both from 74th Amendment — correct.
Confirm Pair 2: 4/5 for DPC vs 2/3 for MPC — DPC threshold is higher — correct.
Confirm Pair 3: MPC for population ≥ 10 lakh; DPC at district level — correct.
Reject Statement 4: Constitution is silent on DPC Chairperson's identity — it does NOT specify an elected representative for DPC; only three statements are correct — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 conflates the MPC Chairperson convention (typically elected) with a non-existent constitutional provision applying to both bodies. Students who know that DPC and MPC are structurally analogous bodies may assume the Chairperson rule is symmetric. In reality, the Constitution leaves the DPC Chairperson's identity entirely to the state legislature, making no such prescription — a critical asymmetry between the two bodies.
solution.final_explanation:
DPC and MPC are companion bodies introduced by the 74th Amendment, but with distinct structural rules.

| Feature | DPC (Art. 243ZD) | MPC (Art. 243ZE) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | District level | Metro area (≥10 lakh) |
| Min. elected | 4/5 | 2/3 |
| Chairperson | Left to state | Typically elected |

• Statement 1 — Correct: Articles 243ZD and 243ZE, both from 74th Amendment.
• Statement 2 — Correct: DPC's 4/5 threshold is more demanding than MPC's 2/3.
• Statement 3 — Correct: MPC's 10-lakh population threshold vs DPC's district-level applicability.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Constitution is silent on DPC Chairperson — this is left to state law. No constitutional prescription for an elected Chairperson in DPC.

Value Addition:
• In practice, District Collectors often chair DPCs in many states — a bureaucratic dominance issue.
• MPC's elected Chairperson requirement reflects the metropolitan-democracy emphasis.
• The different elected-member thresholds (4/5 vs 2/3) are a favourite UPSC data-point comparison.

solution.concept_anchor: Mandatory DPC constitution vs state implementation gap
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because both A and R are factually correct and a student may not pause to verify whether R actually explains why A is true — the causal link needs scrutiny.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Article 243ZD uses 'shall constitute' making DPC mandatory for all states.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. The 74th Amendment provided the constitutional framework but did not include an enforcement mechanism compelling states to actually operationalise DPCs with real powers.
Step 3: Does R explain A? — Yes. The absence of an enforcement mechanism is precisely why the mandatory language coexists with poor implementation — R causally explains the gap described in A.
Both correct and R explains A — answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question tests whether students can distinguish between option (a) and option (b). Both A and R are factually true. The critical question is causation: does the lack of an enforcement mechanism explain why states have failed to constitute functional DPCs despite the mandatory language? Yes — the constitutional compulsion exists but the absence of a penalty or oversight mechanism leaves states free to constitute hollow DPCs or none at all. Students who accept both facts but question the causal link may wrongly choose (b).
solution.final_explanation:
This question probes the tension between constitutional language and constitutional implementation.

Assertion (A): Article 243ZD uses 'shall constitute' — unlike discretionary provisions using 'may', this imposes a mandatory obligation on states. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): The 74th Amendment, while providing the constitutional framework for DPCs, did not incorporate any enforcement mechanism — no provision exists compelling courts or the Union to penalise non-compliant states. This is also factually correct.

Causal link: R directly explains A's paradox. The mandatory constitutional language exists, but states can disregard it without legal consequence because no enforcement architecture was built into the amendment. The 2nd ARC specifically flagged this as a structural failure.

Value Addition:
• Compare with the 91st Amendment (anti-defection) which has a specific enforcement mechanism via the Speaker.
• Many states constitute DPCs on paper without giving them budgets, secretariats, or planning powers.
• Kerala and West Bengal are frequently cited as better performers in DPC operationalisation.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronology of decentralised planning committees
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) swaps the Balwantrai Mehta and Ashok Mehta Committees, which both deal with Panchayati Raj; a student may confuse their sequence.
elimination_logic: Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) is earliest — it recommended democratic decentralisation and three-tier Panchayati Raj.
Ashok Mehta Committee (1978) came next — it recommended two-tier Panchayati Raj and district-level elected planning.
G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) followed — it directly recommended constitutional status for local planning bodies.
L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) is the latest in this pre-amendment sequence — recommended constitutional recognition for Panchayats and local planning; correct order is 1-2-3-4, answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Balwantrai Mehta (1957) and Ashok Mehta (1978) Committees are frequently transposed by students who know both relate to Panchayati Raj but are unsure of sequence. The trap in option (a) exploits this. Additionally, students may confuse G.V.K. Rao (1985) and L.M. Singhvi (1986) as very close in years — the Rao Committee focused on grassroots planning administration while the Singhvi Committee focused on constitutional recognition. Singhvi comes last and most directly preceded the 73rd/74th Amendments of 1992.
solution.final_explanation:
Four key committees shaped the path to constitutional decentralisation culminating in the 73rd and 74th Amendments:

1. Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957): First systematic recommendation for democratic decentralisation and three-tier Panchayati Raj. Recommended Panchayati Raj institutions for planning.
2. Ashok Mehta Committee (1978): Recommended a two-tier structure; emphasised district-level planning through elected bodies.
3. G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): Coined 'grass without roots' critique; recommended constitutional status and planning powers for local bodies.
4. L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): Recommended constitutional recognition for Panchayats; directly influenced the drafting of the 73rd/74th Amendments.

Wrong options swap these chronologically adjacent committees.

Value Addition:
• The L.M. Singhvi Committee's recommendation for constitutional entrenchment is considered the immediate precursor to the 1992 amendments.
• G.V.K. Rao used the phrase 'grass without roots' to describe Panchayati Raj institutions lacking real power.
• The 1992 amendments came 35 years after Balwantrai Mehta's initial recommendations.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 243ZD applicability exemptions tribal scheduled areas
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students know that scheduled areas have special provisions under PESA and may assume DPC provisions simply do not apply there at all, which overstates the exemption.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Part IX-A applies to states — the question concerns a state with Scheduled Areas, not a Union Territory, so the UT exemption is not the primary issue.

Eliminate (b): PESA gives Gram Sabhas enhanced powers in scheduled areas but does not automatically exempt these areas from all DPC provisions — the relationship is complex and states must navigate both.
Eliminate (c): The exemption for states like Nagaland and Mizoram under Part IX-A applies to specific states by name, not to all states merely because they have Sixth Schedule tribal areas.

Confirm (d): States with Fifth Schedule areas must still constitute DPCs under Article 243ZD; however, within those scheduled areas, PESA mandates Gram Sabha consultation — creating a layered obligation, not a blanket exemption.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students aware of PESA and Sixth Schedule provisions often overgeneralise — concluding that any state with tribal or scheduled areas is exempt from DPC provisions. The reality is nuanced: Fifth Schedule areas require PESA compliance alongside DPC obligations. Only specific states named in Part IX-A (Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and certain hill areas) have explicit exemptions. A state in central India with Fifth Schedule districts cannot claim blanket DPC exemption on that basis alone.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243ZD (DPC) is a general provision under Part IX-A. Its applicability in scheduled and tribal areas requires careful analysis.

The scenario involves a state with Fifth Schedule areas (central/eastern India type). Key applicable principles:

• Option (a): Union Territory exemption is inapplicable — this is a state, not a UT.
• Option (b): Overstates the PESA effect. PESA (1996) extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas with customisation for Gram Sabha powers. It does not nullify DPC obligations — the two operate in parallel with PESA taking precedence on matters of tribal customary rights.
• Option (c): Explicit exemptions under Part IX-A exist for specific states (Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram) — these are named exemptions, not a general rule for all tribal-area states.
• Option (d): Correct. A state with Fifth Schedule areas must constitute DPCs but must also ensure that within those areas, the enhanced role of Gram Sabhas under PESA is respected — creating a layered, not mutually exclusive, constitutional obligation.

Value Addition:
• Sixth Schedule areas (Northeast) have Autonomous District Councils — these may functionally overlap with or displace DPC roles.
• PESA Section 4 gives Gram Sabhas powers over natural resources — directly relevant to DPC's environmental conservation mandate.
• States like Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha navigate this DPC-PESA overlap regularly.

solution.concept_anchor: DRDA as non-constitutional body distinct from DPC
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because Zila Parishad is also a district-level body dealing with rural governance, and students may confuse its constitutional basis with DRDA's statutory basis.
elimination_logic: District Planning Committee: constitutional body under Article 243ZD — belongs to the category of constitutionally mandated bodies.
Zila Parishad: constitutional body under Part IX (Panchayats) — belongs to the constitutionally mandated category.
Metropolitan Planning Committee: constitutional body under Article 243ZE — belongs to the constitutionally mandated category.
District Rural Development Agency (DRDA): an administrative/statutory body under the Ministry of Rural Development — NOT a constitutional body; it is the odd one out — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: DRDA and DPC are both district-level bodies involved in development planning, making DRDA a plausible choice that requires precise knowledge. A student who knows DRDA implements rural schemes but does not know its non-constitutional status may include it in the same category as the others. The conflation trap works because DRDA's functions and jurisdiction appear similar to DPC's at the surface — both are district-level development bodies. Only precise knowledge of constitutional vs statutory basis distinguishes them.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests knowledge of the legal basis of district-level bodies.

• Option (a) District Planning Committee: Constitutional body under Article 243ZD, Part IX-A. Mandated by the 74th Amendment.
• Option (b) Zila Parishad: Constitutional body under Part IX (Panchayats), Article 243B. Mandated by the 73rd Amendment as the district-level tier.
• Option (c) District Rural Development Agency (DRDA): Administrative body under the Ministry of Rural Development. It is NOT a constitutional body — created by government executive order to implement rural development schemes like MGNREGS. This is the odd one out.
• Option (d) Metropolitan Planning Committee: Constitutional body under Article 243ZE, Part IX-A.

Value Addition:
• Several committees (including the 2nd ARC) recommended merging DRDA functions with Zila Parishad/DPC to avoid duplication.
• DRDA was initially created under the IRDP programme and later given expanded functions.
• The key distinction is constitutional vs statutory/administrative basis — a recurring UPSC classification test.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC plan forwarding procedure and state obligation

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 243ZD(3), the Chairperson of the District Planning Committee is required to forward the draft development plan to the state government.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZD(3) explicitly states that the Chairperson shall forward the draft plan to the state government — this is a clear procedural constitutional requirement.

statement_analysis.statement: Once the state government receives the draft development plan from the DPC Chairperson, it is constitutionally bound to implement the plan as submitted.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution does not impose any obligation on the state government regarding what it must do after receiving the DPC plan — the state retains full discretion to modify, accept, or disregard it.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) suggesting both statements are correct is deceptive because students may assume that if forwarding is mandatory, implementation must also be mandated — a logical but constitutionally incorrect inference.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Article 243ZD(3) uses 'shall forward' — this is a constitutional mandate on the Chairperson. Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Search for any constitutional provision obligating the state to implement the DPC plan — no such provision exists. The Constitution is silent on what the state must do after receipt.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a logical inference trap. Students correctly know that DPC forwarding is mandatory and may infer, by logical extension, that the receiving state must also be bound. This is a constitutional gap — the amendment created the forwarding obligation but imposed nothing on the receiving government. This asymmetry is precisely what critics cite as making DPC plans non-binding and effectively advisory. A student who reasons from 'mandatory forwarding ∴ mandatory implementation' will incorrectly select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243ZD(3) is one of the most specific — and revealing — provisions relating to DPCs.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Chairperson has a clear constitutional duty to forward the consolidated draft development plan to the state government. This is not discretionary.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No corresponding constitutional obligation falls on the state government. Once the plan is received, the state may incorporate it into state planning, modify it, or effectively set it aside. The Constitution's silence here is the critical implementation gap.

This asymmetry — mandatory forwarding but no mandatory acceptance — is the structural reason why DPC plans often remain advisory. The 2nd ARC and several planning bodies have flagged this as requiring legislative remedy.

Value Addition:
• This gap means DPC plans are constitutionally advisory at the state level — a fundamental weakness.
• Compare with Central Government: DPC plan also cannot be sent directly to Central Government — it must go through the state.
• Reform proposal: Give DPC plans statutory recognition in state planning laws to make them binding inputs.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 243ZD environmental conservation planning mandate
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because 'sustainable development' sounds like the correct constitutional language but is actually a broader policy phrase not used in Article 243ZD itself.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 'Economic growth targets' is an administrative planning concept, not a constitutional mandate in Article 243ZD.
Eliminate (c): 'Sustainable development' is a policy/DPSP-level concept; Article 243ZD uses more specific language.
Eliminate (d): 'Urban housing allocation' is a narrow sectoral function, not one of the DPC's explicit constitutional considerations.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) 'sustainable development' is a sophisticated plausible-fabrication trap. It is a concept closely associated with environmental planning and appears frequently in policy documents, DPSP discussions, and NGT jurisprudence. A student who relies on conceptual familiarity rather than precise constitutional text will prefer it over 'environmental conservation', which is the actual phrase used in Article 243ZD. The distinction matters: 'environmental conservation' is specific and constitutional; 'sustainable development' is broader and not the Article's language.
solution.final_explanation:

• Option (d) 'Urban housing allocation': A specific sectoral function not listed in DPC's constitutional mandate.

• River basin management and forest-fringe planning are practical DPC applications of this mandate.
• The explicit mention of 'natural resources' and 'environmental conservation' makes DPC a constitutionally grounded environmental planning body at the district level.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC financial role — no independent taxing power
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because the State Finance Commission genuinely influences local body finances, and a student may assume this gives DPC some derivative financial authority.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): DPC does not have an independent budget or financial pool — this pairing is incorrect.
Eliminate (b): State Finance Commission recommendations affect local bodies' finances which feed DPC planning, but this does not grant DPC any financial authority — partial truth used to mislead.
Eliminate (c): DPC has no taxing power — taxation belongs to Panchayats and Municipalities under the Constitution, not to DPC.

Confirm (d): DPC's constitutional role is to consolidate financial plans of local bodies and consider 'resources available' — it does not independently allocate, tax, or budget; this pair is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is a partial-truth trap. The State Finance Commission does affect local body finances, and those local bodies' plans feed into DPC consolidation. A student may infer that DPC therefore exercises some financial authority derived from SFC recommendations. But the constitutional reality is that DPC has no financial authority of its own — it only considers available resources as a planning input. Financial power rests with the local bodies themselves, not with DPC.
solution.final_explanation:
DPC's financial role is limited to the planning function — it must consider 'resources available' when consolidating the district plan, but it holds no independent financial power.

• Option (a): Incorrect. DPC has no independent budget. It depends on state grants and devolved funds channelled to Panchayats and Municipalities.
• Option (b): Incorrect as a pairing. While SFC recommendations affect local body finances, they do not grant DPC any financial authority — the SFC-DPC link is indirect.
• Option (c): Incorrect. DPC has no taxing power whatsoever. Taxation powers vest in Panchayats (under state enabling laws) and Municipalities — not in DPC.
• Option (d): Correct. DPC's financial role is strictly to consider 'resources available' as a planning constraint when preparing the draft development plan. It is a planning body, not a financial authority.

Value Addition:
• The absence of independent financial power is a key structural weakness of DPC.
• SFC recommendations under Article 243I (for Panchayats) and Article 243Y (for Municipalities) indirectly shape DPC planning inputs.
• MPLAD funds and Centrally Sponsored Scheme funds often bypass DPC entirely — a noted integration gap.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC implementation gap and collector dominance

statement_analysis.statement: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission highlighted the non-implementation of DPCs as a significant governance failure and recommended providing them with dedicated secretariats and technical support.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2nd ARC specifically flagged DPC non-operationalisation and recommended structural reforms including dedicated secretariats and technical cells for DPCs.

statement_analysis.statement: The institutional tension between the District Collector and the DPC arises because the Collector is constitutionally designated as the de jure planning authority for the district, whereas DPC is merely an advisory body.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional position is the reverse — DPC is the constitutionally designated planning body; the Collector's planning dominance is a de facto reality, not a constitutional designation. No constitutional provision makes the Collector the planning authority.

statement_analysis.statement: Reform proposals have included separating the District Collector's development functions from law and order functions as a way to address the marginalisation of DPCs.
statement_analysis.reason: This separation of functions is a widely discussed reform recommendation to reduce bureaucratic dominance in district planning and give DPCs more space.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming all three are correct is a strong distractor for students who accept Statement 2 without critically examining whether the Collector's planning role is constitutional or merely conventional.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: 2nd ARC's specific recommendation on DPC secretariat and technical support is documented — correct.
Reject Statement 2: This reverses the constitutional position. DPC is the de jure planning authority; Collector's dominance is de facto and unconstitutional in intent — this statement is wrong.
Confirm Statement 3: Separation of Collector's functions is a standard reform recommendation — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 employs reversed-causation combined with scope-extension. Students familiar with the Collector's actual dominance in district planning may accept the claim that the Collector is the 'constitutionally designated' planning authority — since that is the ground reality. The trap is in conflating de facto practice with constitutional designation. The Constitution actually designates DPC as the planning body; the Collector's role is purely executive and administrative, not a constitutional planning designation.
solution.final_explanation:
The DPC-Collector dynamic represents one of Indian governance's most persistent constitutional-versus-practice tensions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 2nd ARC specifically identified DPC non-implementation as a governance failure and recommended dedicated secretariats, technical support, and clearly defined planning powers for DPCs.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement reverses the constitutional reality. DPC is the constitutionally mandated district planning body; the District Collector has no constitutional designation as planning authority. The Collector's dominance is a product of colonial administrative legacy and executive inertia, not constitutional intent.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The recommendation to separate development administration from law and order is meant to create a distinct development executive accountable to elected bodies like DPC, reducing bureaucratic capture of district planning.

Value Addition:
• The IAS officer's control over district development predates Independence — an enduring legacy of the colonial district administration model.
• Kerala's model of elected chairpersons for DPCs is cited as a corrective.
• The reform debate connects to the broader question of 'District Government' as envisaged in 2nd ARC Report.

solution.concept_anchor: Mandatory vs discretionary language Article 243ZD

statement_analysis.statement: Article 243ZD uses the word 'may', giving state governments the discretion to constitute or not constitute District Planning Committees depending on their administrative needs.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZD uses 'shall constitute', not 'may' — DPC constitution is mandatory, not discretionary for state governments.

statement_analysis.statement: The District Planning Committee is a statutory body created under the provisions of the Municipal Laws Amendment Act, 1993, not a constitutional body.
statement_analysis.reason: DPC is a constitutional body created directly by Article 243ZD of the Constitution, not by any statute. Its constitutional status is a fundamental characteristic.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) suggesting both statements are correct is a double-trap: students who confuse 'shall' with 'may' and believe DPC is statutory will choose (c).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 243ZD uses 'shall constitute' — this is mandatory language. The 'may' characterisation is false. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: DPC derives its existence from Article 243ZD of the Constitution itself — not from any statute. Calling it a statutory body is factually wrong. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Both statements are incorrect — the question asks which are NOT correct — answer is (c) Both 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the 'shall vs may' distinction that UPSC frequently tests across multiple constitutional provisions. Students who know DPCs are poorly implemented may incorrectly infer that the provision must be discretionary ('may'). Statement 2 exploits the constitutional vs statutory body distinction — a fundamental classification that students sometimes misapply to DPC by associating it with local body laws passed by state legislatures after 1992.
solution.final_explanation:
Two foundational facts about DPC's constitutional character are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 243ZD employs 'shall constitute' — the language of constitutional compulsion, not discretion. Compare this with provisions using 'may' (like some provisions for ward committees). The mandatory language is precisely why non-constitution of DPCs is a constitutional violation, not merely a policy failure.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: DPC is unambiguously a constitutional body — it draws its existence and mandate directly from Article 243ZD. No statute created DPC. State legislatures may enact laws to operationalise DPC details, but the body itself is constitutional in origin.

Value Addition:
• 'Shall' vs 'may' in the Constitution is a recurrent UPSC distinction — Article 243ZD (DPC) uses 'shall'; compare with Article 243S (Ward Committees) which also uses 'shall' for municipalities above 3 lakh population.
• Constitutional bodies cannot be abolished by state statute alone — they require constitutional amendment.
• The DPC's constitutional status means a writ petition can be filed against a state for failing to constitute it.

solution.concept_anchor: PESA and Sixth Schedule DPC applicability distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because Sixth Schedule areas do have autonomous district councils with planning-like functions, making students conflate these with DPC exemptions under Part IX-A.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): PESA extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas — it does not abolish DPC obligations; Fifth Schedule states still have DPC obligations.

Eliminate (b): Sixth Schedule areas have autonomous district councils, but the specific states exempt under Part IX-A (Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram) are named explicitly — not all Sixth Schedule states.
Eliminate (d): DPC provisions apply to states, not UTs — Parliament may extend to UTs separately; this option conflates UT extension with Sixth Schedule exemption.

Confirm (c): The Constitution explicitly names certain states — Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and specified hill areas — as exempt from Part IX-A provisions including DPC; these are the precise exemptions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with the Sixth Schedule may conflate all Sixth Schedule areas with the specific states named in Part IX-A exemptions. The Constitution names specific states (primarily those with extensive tribal governance structures) as exempt from Part IX-A. These states have autonomous district councils under the Sixth Schedule that serve planning-like functions. However, not all Sixth Schedule states or areas are exempt — only those specifically named. This precision is the core of the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Part IX-A (which includes Article 243ZD) contains explicit exemptions for specific states and territories.

• Option (a): PESA extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas — it does not exempt these areas from DPC provisions. Fifth Schedule states in central India (Jharkhand, Odisha, etc.) are not exempt.
• Option (b): Sixth Schedule tribal areas have autonomous district councils, but Part IX-A exemptions are not automatic for all Sixth Schedule states — they apply only to named states.
• Option (c): Correct. The Constitution explicitly exempts states like Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and specified hill district areas (like certain areas of Manipur and certain districts of Assam) from Part IX-A provisions — including DPC. These exemptions reflect the existence of pre-existing tribal governance structures.
• Option (d): Union Territories are separately handled — Parliament may extend Part IX-A to UTs by law. This is distinct from the Sixth Schedule exemption issue.

Value Addition:
• Nagaland's exemption reflects the Naga customary law protection under Article 371A.
• These exemptions are built into Part IX-A itself, not added later by amendment.
• The existence of elected village/clan councils in these areas was the constitutional rationale for exemption.

solution.concept_anchor: 74th Amendment DPC as culmination of decentralisation committees
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are correct, but students may rush to choose (a) without pausing to check whether the Balwantrai Mehta Committee recommendation specifically and causally led to the 74th Amendment's DPC provision.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Before the 74th Amendment (1992), district planning was entirely executive — no elected body had a constitutional mandate for district planning.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. The Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) was the first to recommend democratic decentralisation and participatory local planning, initiating a 35-year reform journey.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Not directly. The Balwantrai Mehta Committee's recommendations (1957) explain the intellectual origins of decentralised planning, but the immediate cause of the pre-74th Amendment situation being exclusively bureaucratic was the lack of constitutional mandate — not the Mehta Committee's existence. R is a historical precursor, not the direct explanation of A.
Both correct but R does NOT causally explain A — answer is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
This question requires careful causal reasoning between two true facts.

Assertion (A): Before the 74th Amendment, district planning was exclusively an executive-bureaucratic function. No elected body had a constitutional mandate for district development planning. This is historically accurate.

Reason (R): The Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) did initiate India's modern thinking on democratic decentralisation and was the first major committee to recommend elected Panchayati Raj institutions with planning functions. This is also factually correct.

Causal link analysis: R describes the historical origin of the decentralisation idea, not the cause of the pre-74th Amendment bureaucratic status of district planning. The pre-amendment bureaucratic dominance was caused by the absence of a constitutional mandate — not by the Mehta Committee's recommendations. In fact, the Mehta Committee argued FOR the change that eventually came. So R is a contributing intellectual precursor, not an explanation of A's state of affairs.

Value Addition:
• 1957–1992: 35 years elapsed between Balwantrai Mehta's recommendations and their constitutional realisation.
• The Ashok Mehta, G.V.K. Rao, and L.M. Singhvi Committees were intermediate steps in this reform journey.
• The 74th Amendment simultaneously created Municipalities, Ward Committees, DPCs, and MPCs — a package reform.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC unique rural-urban integration mandate

statement_analysis.statement: DPC is the only body constitutionally mandated to integrate development plans of both Panchayats and Municipalities at the district level.
statement_analysis.reason: No other constitutional body is mandated to integrate rural (Panchayat) and urban (Municipal) plans at the district level — this is DPC's unique constitutional function.

statement_analysis.statement: The NITI Aayog performs the same rural-urban plan integration function as DPC but at the national level, making DPC redundant for larger districts.
statement_analysis.reason: NITI Aayog functions at the national/state level and does not have a constitutional mandate for rural-urban integration at the district level. DPC's function is unique and district-specific.

statement_analysis.statement: The DPC's rural-urban integration mandate explicitly extends to peri-urban areas, shared water bodies, and migration-related planning.
statement_analysis.reason: While these are practical applications of DPC's integration mandate, the Constitution does not explicitly name peri-urban areas or migration in Article 243ZD — it uses broader language about shared natural resources and common infrastructure.

statement_analysis.statement: A practical challenge in DPC's rural-urban integration function is the asymmetric planning capacity between urban local bodies and gram panchayats.
statement_analysis.reason: Urban local bodies typically have more administrative capacity and resources for plan preparation compared to gram panchayats — this asymmetry is a documented challenge in DPC functioning.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) suggesting only two are correct may seem right to students who accept Statement 3 (peri-urban planning) as obviously true given DPC's spatial mandate.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: DPC's unique constitutional integration mandate is well-established — correct.
Reject Statement 2: NITI Aayog does not perform district-level rural-urban integration — it is a national planning body without this constitutional mandate.
Reject Statement 3: The Constitution uses 'shared natural resources' and 'common infrastructure' — not explicit references to peri-urban areas or migration. Scope-extension makes this incorrect.
Confirm Statement 4: Asymmetric capacity between urban and rural local bodies is a documented governance reality — correct. Only two correct (Statements 1 and 4) — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the scope-extension trap. Students who correctly understand DPC's spatial mandate may extrapolate to assume that peri-urban areas and migration are explicitly mentioned constitutional considerations. The Constitution uses broader language ('shared natural resources,' 'common interest') — the specific applications like peri-urban and migration are implicit, not explicit. Treating implicit applications as explicit constitutional text is the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
DPC's rural-urban integration is its most distinctive constitutional feature.

• Statement 1 — Correct: DPC is constitutionally unique in mandating integration of both Panchayat and Municipal plans at the district level. No other body has this dual mandate.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: NITI Aayog operates at national and state level. It has no constitutional mandate for district-level rural-urban plan integration. Comparing it to DPC conflates different levels of governance.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Constitution's language is general — 'matters of common interest including spatial planning, sharing of physical and natural resources, integrated infrastructure development, and environmental conservation.' Peri-urban and migration are not explicitly named.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The asymmetric planning capacity between urban local bodies (with larger tax bases and technical staff) and gram panchayats (often under-resourced) is a real implementation challenge.

Value Addition:
• DPC's rural-urban mandate is increasingly relevant given India's rapid urbanisation and peri-urban sprawl.
• The urban-rural continuum is a planning concept where DPC could play a crucial coordinating role.
• Only Statements 1 and 4 are correct — answer is (b) Only two.

solution.concept_anchor: 2nd ARC DPC reform recommendations

statement_analysis.statement: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended that DPCs be provided with dedicated secretariats and technical support cells to address the lack of planning expertise among elected members.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2nd ARC specifically identified the lack of technical capacity and secretariat support as a reason for DPC dysfunction and made this a central recommendation.

statement_analysis.statement: A proposal to link MPLAD scheme funds with the DPC planning framework has been debated as a mechanism to improve fund-plan integration at the district level.
statement_analysis.reason: Linking MPLAD funds with DPC planning is a documented reform debate to align parliamentary constituency-level spending with district plans — though not yet implemented.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2nd ARC recommended abolishing District Planning Committees and replacing them with strengthened District Collectors with planning powers to improve implementation efficiency.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2nd ARC recommended strengthening DPCs, not abolishing them. It advocated for more representative and empowered DPCs — the opposite of bureaucratising planning through the Collector.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) claiming all three correct is deceptive for students who cannot recall whether the 2nd ARC recommended abolition or strengthening — the authoritative-sounding statement about 'implementation efficiency' makes Statement 3 plausible.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: 2nd ARC's recommendation for DPC secretariats and technical cells is a standard governance fact — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: MPLAD-DPC integration is a documented reform proposal — correct.

Reject Statement 3: The 2nd ARC's entire thrust was to strengthen elected local governance including DPCs — recommending abolition in favour of Collector power would contradict its entire philosophy. This is a plausible-fabrication trap.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap. The idea of strengthening the District Collector for 'implementation efficiency' sounds like a reasonable administrative recommendation and students who are unsure about the 2nd ARC's specific DPC stance may accept it. The 2nd ARC's actual position was the opposite — it wanted DPCs empowered with real planning authority, technical support, and democratic legitimacy, not replaced by bureaucratic authority.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2nd ARC (submitted reports between 2005–2009) addressed local governance comprehensively and DPC reform specifically.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Dedicated secretariats and technical planning cells were central to the 2nd ARC's DPC reform agenda. Elected members lack urban planning, environmental assessment, and financial modelling skills — technical cells address this.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The MPLAD-DPC integration debate is genuine. MPs spend funds on local infrastructure that often overlaps with or contradicts DPC plans — integration would improve coherence. This remains unimplemented.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The 2nd ARC never recommended abolishing DPCs. Its consistent position was empowering DPCs with real powers, budgets, and technical support. Replacing DPCs with Collector-led planning would reverse the decentralisation agenda the 2nd ARC championed.

Value Addition:
• The 2nd ARC's Report on Local Governance (6th Report) is the key reference for DPC reform prescriptions.
• Overlapping jurisdiction between DPC, state planning departments, and line ministries is the central coordination challenge.
• MPLAD funds (₹5 crore/MP/year) are a significant but DPC-unaligned source of district infrastructure spending.

statement_analysis.statement: The abolition of the Planning Commission in 2014 and its replacement by NITI Aayog weakened the institutional linkage between DPC district plans and national five-year planning cycles, since NITI Aayog does not prepare binding five-year plans.
statement_analysis.reason: The Planning Commission's five-year plans provided a framework into which district plans theoretically fed; NITI Aayog, which does not prepare binding national plans, removed this framework — weakening the top-down anchoring for DPC plans.

statement_analysis.statement: The Planning Commission was abolished by a constitutional amendment in 2014, necessitating the insertion of NITI Aayog provisions into the same Part of the Constitution that houses DPC provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: The Planning Commission was an executive body created by a Cabinet Resolution (1950) — it was never a constitutional body. It was dissolved by executive order in 2014, not by constitutional amendment. NITI Aayog is also an executive body, not constitutionally established.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) suggesting both statements are correct is deceptive because Statement 2 sounds procedurally accurate to students who may not know the Planning Commission's non-constitutional status.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Planning Commission was abolished in 2014 by executive order; NITI Aayog replaced it without binding plan-making authority — the institutional linkage for DPC bottom-up planning was indeed weakened. Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Check whether Planning Commission was constitutional — it was established by a Cabinet Resolution in 1950, not by the Constitution. It was dissolved by executive order, not constitutional amendment. NITI Aayog is also not constitutional. Statement 2 is factually incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common conflation between major governmental bodies and constitutional status. Many students assume that a body as important as the Planning Commission must have had constitutional backing. In reality, it was an entirely executive creation by Cabinet Resolution — a point UPSC has tested in multiple years. The statement's specific mention of 'constitutional amendment' and 'same Part of the Constitution' sounds procedurally plausible, making it an effective trap.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the intersection of planning institutional history and constitutional law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Planning Commission's five-year plans created a framework within which district plans (through DPCs) were supposed to feed upward into state plans and then into national plans. NITI Aayog, having no mandate to prepare binding national plans, removed this anchor — weakening the bottom-up planning rationale for DPCs.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Planning Commission was created by a Cabinet Resolution of the Government of India in March 1950. It had no constitutional basis. Its dissolution in January 2015 was by executive order (not constitutional amendment). NITI Aayog was similarly established by executive resolution — it is not constitutionally recognised.

Value Addition:
• Planning Commission: 1950–2014 (executive body under Cabinet Resolution).
• NITI Aayog: January 1, 2015 onwards (executive body by Cabinet Resolution).
• The absence of binding five-year plans is a major structural change affecting DPC's planning relevance.
• DPC's bottom-up planning philosophy requires a receptive top-down structure — currently missing.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC Chairperson constitutional silence vs MPC
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) stating the Constitution designates the elected Mayor as DPC Chairperson swaps MPC's conventional Chairperson arrangement onto DPC — a classic entity-swap for students who study MPC and DPC together.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): The elected Mayor as Chairperson is associated with MPC, not DPC — entity-swap trap.
Eliminate (c): District Collector as mandatory constitutional Chairperson is incorrect — the Constitution does not specify this; it is practice in some states, not a constitutional requirement.
Eliminate (d): Finance Secretary as ex-officio Chairperson is a plausible fabrication — no constitutional provision for this.
Confirm (a): The Constitution does not specify who shall be the DPC Chairperson — this is left to the state legislature, making (a) correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in option (b) is the primary trap. Students who study DPC and MPC together know that the MPC Chairperson is envisaged as elected and associate this with the democratic spirit of both bodies. Transferring the MPC Chairperson convention to DPC creates a plausible but incorrect answer. The constitutional reality is that DPC's Chairperson is not specified — only the state legislature determines this, creating wide variation in practice across states.
solution.final_explanation:
The Constitution's silence on DPC Chairperson identity is a notable structural feature.

• Option (a): Correct. Article 243ZD does not specify who shall be the Chairperson. This is explicitly left to the state legislature. States therefore vary — some appoint elected representatives, others the District Collector.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The elected Mayor as Chairperson is a feature associated with Metropolitan Planning Committees, not DPC. This is the entity-swap trap.
• Option (c): Incorrect. While the District Collector chairs DPCs in many states as a matter of practice, this is not a constitutional requirement — it is a state legislative or executive choice.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Finance Secretary as ex-officio Chairperson is a fabricated option — no constitutional or standard statutory provision supports this.

Value Addition:
• The DPC Chairperson's identity affects the body's character: an elected chair makes DPC more democratic; a Collector chair makes it more bureaucratic.
• Kerala uses elected representatives as DPC Chairpersons — cited as a democratic best practice.
• Article 243ZD(3) refers to 'the Chairperson of such Committee' when specifying the plan-forwarding duty — confirming existence of a Chairperson without specifying identity.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC environmental conservation mandate and Article 48A linkage
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are factually correct and the causal relationship sounds plausible, but R explains the legal basis for the environmental mandate, not why river basin management is specifically relevant.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Article 243ZD explicitly requires DPCs to consider environmental conservation and natural resource sharing — river basin management, forest-fringe areas, and coastal zones are direct practical applications.

Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Article 48A (DPSP for environment protection) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty to protect environment) do exist and are part of the constitutional environmental framework.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — Partially, but not directly. A is about DPC's specific constitutional mandate in Article 243ZD itself. The environmental mandate comes from Article 243ZD's own text — not primarily from Articles 48A and 51A(g). R describes related provisions, not the cause of A.
Both correct but R is not the direct explanation of A — answer is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
This question requires precise causal reasoning between DPC's constitutional environmental mandate and related constitutional provisions.

Assertion (A): Article 243ZD's explicit mention of 'matters of common interest including... environmental conservation' makes DPC directly relevant to multi-local-body environmental challenges like river basin management. This is factually accurate — multiple Panchayats and Municipalities sharing a river basin is precisely the kind of challenge DPC is constitutionally designed to coordinate.

Reason (R): Articles 48A and 51A(g) are real constitutional provisions. Article 48A (DPSP) directs the state to protect and improve the environment; Article 51A(g) is the fundamental duty to protect the natural environment. Both are genuine constitutional provisions.

Causal analysis: A's environmental mandate stems directly from Article 243ZD's own text — DPC's duty is self-contained within 243ZD. Articles 48A and 51A(g) represent complementary constitutional environmental values but are not the source of DPC's specific planning mandate. R provides context, not causation.

Value Addition:
• Article 48A is a DPSP in Part IV; Article 51A(g) is a Fundamental Duty in Part IV-A — neither is directly enforceable but both inform judicial interpretation.
• The Supreme Court in MC Mehta cases has used Articles 48A and 21 to develop environmental law — the 'right to a clean environment' flows from Article 21.
• DPC's environmental mandate could theoretically ground environmental impact assessment at the district planning level.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 243ZD elected member minimum fraction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) using 'two-thirds' is deceptive because two-thirds is the elected minimum for MPCs — students who study DPC and MPC together may substitute the MPC fraction for the DPC fraction.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): One-half is too low and not a constitutionally specified fraction for either DPC or MPC.
Eliminate (b): Two-thirds is the minimum for MPC (Article 243ZE), not DPC — temporal-swap of the fraction between the two bodies.
Eliminate (d): Three-fourths is not the constitutionally specified fraction for DPC — a plausible distractor close to 4/5.
Confirm (c): Article 243ZD(2) uses 'not less than four-fifths' — this is the correct fraction for DPC elected members.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is a precision trap exploiting the DPC-MPC comparison. Students who study both bodies often know that MPC requires 2/3 elected members and DPC requires a higher fraction but may confuse which fraction (4/5) applies to DPC. Presenting 2/3 as an option directly exploits this confusion — a student who has partially memorised the comparison will choose 2/3 for DPC rather than 4/5.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243ZD(2) specifies the minimum elected membership of DPCs with constitutional precision.

• Option (a) One-half: Not the constitutional fraction — too permissive and not specified in Article 243ZD.
• Option (b) Two-thirds: This is the constitutional minimum for Metropolitan Planning Committees under Article 243ZE — not for DPCs. A classic substitution trap.
• Option (c) Four-fifths: Correct. Article 243ZD(2) uses 'not less than four-fifths' — meaning at least 80% of DPC members must be elected from Panchayat and Municipal members. This is the highest elected-proportion requirement among comparable bodies.
• Option (d) Three-fourths: A plausible approximation (75%) that is close to 4/5 (80%) but constitutionally incorrect.

Value Addition:
• DPC's 4/5 threshold (80%) > MPC's 2/3 threshold (67%) — DPC requires proportionally more elected representation.
• The higher elected fraction reflects DPC's wider rural-urban integration mandate covering larger populations.
• This constitutional fraction is among the most frequently tested DPC data points in competitive examinations.

solution.concept_anchor: DRDA non-constitutional status vs DPC constitutional body
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because it correctly identifies DRDA's Ministry link but pairs it with 'constitutional body' status — students who know DRDA is under Ministry of Rural Development may accept this without questioning the constitutional body claim.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): DPC does not have independent taxing power or its own budget — this pairing is incorrect.
Eliminate (c): DRDA is correctly linked to Ministry of Rural Development but it is NOT a constitutional body — conflation trap.
Eliminate (d): The merger recommendation is attributed to several committees, not exclusively to the NITI Aayog — factual inaccuracy.
Confirm (b): DPC is a constitutional body under Article 243ZD; DRDA is an administrative body under Ministry of Rural Development — the distinction in legal basis is correctly and completely stated.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) is the conflation trap. DRDA's association with the Ministry of Rural Development is accurate, but appending 'constitutional body' status to it is false. Students who correctly know DRDA's administrative connection may not specifically recall that DRDA has no constitutional basis — accepting the first half of the pairing while missing the false second half is the trap mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
The DPC-DRDA distinction is fundamental to understanding India's district development architecture.

• Option (a): Incorrect. DPC has no independent taxing power or budget — its financial role is to consider available resources, not to control them.
• Option (b): Correct. DPC is a constitutional body under Article 243ZD, mandating integrated district-level planning. DRDA is an administrative body created to implement Ministry of Rural Development schemes — it has no constitutional status.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Ministry of Rural Development link for DRDA is correct, but DRDA is not a constitutional body — it was created by executive action.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The merger recommendation has been made by multiple committees and bodies, not exclusively NITI Aayog.

Value Addition:
• DRDA covers only rural areas; DPC covers both rural and urban areas — a key functional difference.
• Several states have wound up DRDAs and merged their functions with Zila Parishads — a partial implementation of merger recommendations.
• DPC-DRDA duplication is most acute in districts receiving large central rural development fund flows.

solution.concept_anchor: State legislature DPC operationalisation and implementation gap

statement_analysis.statement: While Article 243ZD mandates the constitution of DPCs, the details of composition beyond the constitutional minimum, the specific powers, and the functions of DPCs are left to the state legislature to prescribe by law.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZD establishes the constitutional framework but explicitly leaves detailed composition, powers, and functions to state legislation — creating constitutionally valid state variation.

statement_analysis.statement: States like Kerala and West Bengal have been cited as relatively better performers in operationalising DPCs with genuine planning functions, compared to the majority of states.
statement_analysis.reason: Kerala and West Bengal are consistently cited in governance literature as states that have given DPCs more meaningful planning roles, in contrast to many other states with dormant or nominal DPCs.

statement_analysis.statement: Since the Constitution mandates DPC constitution using the word 'shall', any state that fails to constitute a functional DPC can be penalised by the Election Commission of India by deferring local body elections.
statement_analysis.reason: The Election Commission has no constitutional authority to penalise states for DPC non-constitution. The ECI's jurisdiction relates to elections, not to the constitution of planning bodies. There is no enforcement mechanism for DPC compliance.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because the mandatory 'shall' language makes Statement 3's penalisation claim sound logically consistent — students who know DPC is mandatory may believe a penalty mechanism must exist.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: State legislature's role in filling out DPC details is explicitly provided — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: Kerala and West Bengal's better performance on DPC operationalisation is well-documented — correct.
Reject Statement 3: ECI has no role in enforcing DPC constitution — its mandate is elections. Scope-extension of mandatory language into a non-existent penalty mechanism.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a scope-extension trap that combines two correct facts — DPC is mandatory, and the ECI enforces constitutional requirements — but misattributes the enforcement to an institution with no such mandate. The ECI enforces election schedules and related constitutional provisions. DPC non-constitution is a state constitutional failure but there is no enforcement institution for it. Students who correctly know the ECI's role in local body elections (under SERC/SERC provisions) may extend this to DPC compliance — an unjustified extension.
solution.final_explanation:
State legislatures have both the responsibility and discretion to give DPCs their detailed operational character.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 243ZD is a constitutional framework provision. States must constitute DPCs (mandatory) but have legislative discretion on detailed composition, powers, and functions beyond constitutional minimums.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Among Indian states, Kerala (with its People's Planning Campaign) and West Bengal have historically given DPCs more substantive roles. Most other states have dormant or symbolic DPCs.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Election Commission of India's mandate under the Constitution is electoral — it has no jurisdiction over DPC constitution. The State Election Commission handles local body elections, but even the SEC has no power over DPC compliance. No constitutional enforcement mechanism exists for DPC non-constitution.

Value Addition:
• Kerala's People's Planning Campaign (1996) transferred 35-40% of the state plan to local bodies, giving DPCs meaningful plans to consolidate.
• The SEC (State Election Commission) under Article 243K oversees local body elections — distinct from DPC constitution which is the state legislature's responsibility.
• The absence of enforcement is why Article 243ZD's 'shall' remains aspirational for most states.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence of pre-amendment DPC-related developments
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive by placing PESA before the 74th Amendment, which students who know PESA came after 1992 might recognise as wrong but may still second-guess because PESA deals with tribal areas that had pre-existing autonomy.
elimination_logic: Event 1 must be first: G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) preceded the L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) — both pre-amendment.
Event 2 follows: L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) came after G.V.K. Rao Committee.
Event 3 follows: 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992/1993) institutionalised DPC provisions.
Event 4 is last: PESA (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act was enacted in 1996 — after the 74th Amendment. Correct order: G.V.K. Rao → L.M. Singhvi → 74th Amendment → PESA. Answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is the G.V.K. Rao (1985) vs L.M. Singhvi (1986) sequence — a one-year gap that students may reverse. Both committees are associated with local governance reform, making their precise chronological order difficult to recall without specific year knowledge. Additionally, students who know PESA dealt with tribal areas (which predate the 74th Amendment in terms of political history) might incorrectly place it earlier in the sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
Four key milestones in the path from decentralised planning advocacy to tribal area application:

1. G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): Recommended constitutional status and planning powers for local bodies; coined 'grass without roots' critique.
2. L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): Recommended constitutional recognition for Panchayats; directly influenced the 73rd/74th Amendment drafting.
3. 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992, in force April 1993): Inserted Part IX-A, created DPC under Article 243ZD.
4. PESA Act, 1996: Extended Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule tribal areas with modifications for Gram Sabha powers.

The correct sequence is 1-2-3-4. Wrong options place PESA before the 74th Amendment or reverse the Rao-Singhvi sequence.

Value Addition:
• G.V.K. Rao Committee was appointed by the Planning Commission — making it the only planning-commission-appointed committee in this sequence.
• PESA was enacted by Parliament under Article 243M(4) — a special provision for Scheduled Areas.
• The year gap between the 74th Amendment (1992) and PESA (1996) meant Scheduled Areas were without tailored Panchayat provisions for four years.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC bottom-up planning vs centrally sponsored scheme bypass
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because MPLAD funds are indeed spent at the district level, and a student may incorrectly believe MPLAD money flows through the DPC framework when it actually bypasses it entirely.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): DPC's draft plan goes to the state government, not the Central Government directly — and the scenario concerns state-level scheme implementation, not DPC-to-Centre linkage.
Eliminate (b): MPLAD funds are spent by MPs on constituency infrastructure and bypass DPC entirely — MPLAD funds do NOT flow through DPC. This is a well-documented bypass.
Eliminate (c): The DPC's constitutional mandate does NOT give it power to reject or veto centrally sponsored schemes — it has no such authority.

Confirm (d): The scenario correctly illustrates the 'bypass problem' — centrally sponsored schemes are designed and funded at the Centre, implemented by district administration, and typically ignore DPC plans. This is the core gap between decentralised planning ideal and CSS reality.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is a partial-truth trap. MPLAD funds are indeed linked to district development and MPs are elected representatives. A student who knows that reform proposals suggest linking MPLAD with DPC (Statement 2 of an earlier question) may mistakenly believe this link already exists. In reality, MPLAD funds bypass DPC entirely — the reform proposal exists precisely because this bypass is a problem, not because integration is already in place.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the gap between decentralised planning theory (DPC) and centralised implementation reality (CSS).

The applicable principle is the 'bottom-up planning bypass' — a structural weakness where centrally sponsored schemes are designed at the national level with uniform guidelines, implemented by district administration following Central and State instructions, and do not require alignment with or endorsement by the DPC's draft development plan.

• Option (a): Incorrect. DPC plans go to state government, not directly to the Centre. Moreover, the central problem here is scheme implementation bypassing DPC, not the forwarding route.
• Option (b): Incorrect. MPLAD funds bypass DPC entirely — they are controlled by elected MPs through district administration, with no DPC oversight or integration. The reform proposal to link them exists because integration is absent.
• Option (c): Incorrect. DPC has no constitutional power to reject or modify centrally sponsored schemes — it has no such veto or oversight authority.
• Option (d): Correct. The scenario illustrates the core tension: DPC is mandated to consolidate district plans bottom-up, but centrally sponsored schemes arrive top-down with predetermined guidelines, bypassing the DPC framework entirely.

Value Addition:
• Centrally sponsored schemes account for a large proportion of district development spending — making DPC plan relevance marginal in practice.
• The BRGF (Backward Regions Grant Fund) was theoretically meant to be channelled through district plans but also suffered implementation gaps.
• True decentralised planning requires CSS guidelines to be flexible enough to align with DPC plans — currently rare.

solution.concept_anchor: DPC plan matters — constitutional vs non-constitutional considerations
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 'integration of rural and urban infrastructure' sounds like a broad policy goal not specifically linked to DPC, when in fact it is explicitly part of the constitutional mandate.
elimination_logic: Option (a) — spatial planning: Explicitly mentioned in Article 243ZD as a matter DPC must consider — belongs.
Option (b) — integrated infrastructure development: Explicitly mentioned in Article 243ZD as a matter DPC must consider — belongs.
Option (c) — sharing of physical and natural resources between Panchayats and Municipalities: Explicitly mentioned in Article 243ZD — belongs.

Option (d) — regulation of land use and building permissions: This is a function listed in the Twelfth Schedule (functions of Municipalities) and is a local body function, NOT one of the specific matters Article 243ZD lists for DPC consideration — does not belong in the same constitutional category.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the strong distractor — 'integrated infrastructure development' is constitutional DPC language but sounds like a generic policy phrase. Students may incorrectly treat it as the odd one out. Option (d) is the correct odd one out: regulation of land use is a Twelfth Schedule municipal function, not a matter listed under Article 243ZD for DPC's draft plan consideration. The trap exploits the overlap between DPC planning functions and municipal regulatory functions.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243ZD specifies which matters must be considered by DPCs when preparing the draft development plan.

• Option (a) Spatial planning: Explicitly listed in Article 243ZD's mandate for DPC consideration — belongs in the DPC mandate category.
• Option (b) Integrated infrastructure development: Also explicitly listed in Article 243ZD — belongs, despite sounding like generic policy language.
• Option (c) Sharing of physical and natural resources: Directly stated in Article 243ZD as a matter of common interest DPC must consider — belongs.
• Option (d) Regulation of land use and building permissions: This is a function of Municipalities listed in Item 1 of the Twelfth Schedule — it is a regulatory/governance function of local bodies, not one of the matters Article 243ZD mandates DPC to consider in its draft plan. This is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 functions for Municipalities — regulation of land use is Item 1.
• DPC's role is to integrate plans, not to regulate — regulation remains with local bodies.
• Article 243ZD's listed considerations: spatial planning, natural resource sharing, integrated infrastructure, and environmental conservation — memorise these four.
